questions.explain: Three scenarios: A (high read ratio, repetitive queries — catalogs, profiles, sessions) → cache wins overwhelmingly; B (write-heavy transactional — orders, event logging) → cache adds cost without benefit; C (mixed, 80% of reads hit 20% of rows — the most common pattern) → nuanced optimization. Cache ROI = database instance savings/month − cache cost/month — e.g., db.r5.2xlarge at $1,400/mo → r5.xlarge at $700/mo after offload, with a cache.r6g.large at $104/mo netting ~$600/mo.
options: High read ratio + repetitive queries → cache wins; write-heavy transactional → cache adds cost; mixed with hot concentration → nuanced; ROI = DB savings − cache cost — e.g., $1,400→$700/mo instance with a $104/mo cache nets ~$600/mo
questions.q: When does a caching layer pay for itself, and what is the ROI formula?

questions.explain: Size from the hot working set (a 500GB database may have only 8–12GB hot), not total DB size, and target 75–80% memory utilization for replication/expiration headroom; node mapping: 2–6GB → r6g.large ($104/mo), 6–24GB → r6g.xlarge ($208/mo), etc. 1-year RIs cut 40–45%, 3-year up to 55% — reserved pricing is correct for any cluster running >6 months.
options: Size the cache to total database size
Always use the largest node available
Size to the hot working set (often a small fraction of DB size), target 75–80% memory utilization, and use reserved pricing (40–45% off 1-yr) for clusters running >6 months
questions.q: How should ElastiCache clusters be sized for cost efficiency?

questions.explain: Break-even hit rate is ~60–70%; the sweet spot is 85%+ — at 80% hit rate a db.r5.4xlarge ($5,600/mo) can drop to r6g.2xlarge ($1,752) + cache ($208) = $1,544/mo savings, and at 95% → r6g.xlarge ($876) + cache = $2,420/mo savings, so the 80→95% gap is worth ~$900/mo. Monitor via metric-math alarm on CacheHits/(Hits+Misses) firing below 80%, and watch Evictions as the leading indicator of memory pressure.
options: 85%+ is the sweet spot (break-even ~60–70%); the 80→95% gap can be worth ~$900/mo on a large instance; alarm below 80% hit rate and watch evictions as the leading indicator
Any hit rate above 10% is fine
Only monitor CPU, not hit rate
questions.q: What cache hit rate is needed for caching to pay off, and how is it monitored?

questions.explain: Four causes of hit rate degradation: TTL too short (a profile queried every 15 min with a 5-min TTL never hits); key space explosion (unnormalized parameters doubling key count); memory pressure evictions (check Evictions metric; allkeys-lru is typically correct for caching); deployments flushing the cache (hit rates recover as warming completes).
options: TTL too short, key space explosion from unnormalized parameters, memory-pressure evictions (check Evictions; use allkeys-lru), and post-deploy cache flushes awaiting warm-up
questions.q: What are the four causes of cache hit rate degradation?

questions.explain: L1 in-process cache (e.g., lru_cache, 256MB) absorbs the top 5–10% hottest keys at zero infrastructure cost, L2 ElastiCache Redis handles the next tier, and RDS serves only misses — but the gotcha is that 20 app instances = 20 independent caches and TTL clocks, so use short L1 TTLs (30–120s) with longer Redis TTLs, accepting brief inconsistency windows. Invalidation: over-invalidation (cache stays cold, you pay without savings — the more common failure) vs under-invalidation (stale data → incidents/credits); align TTL to business staleness tolerance per data class.
options: L1 in-process (free, short 30–120s TTLs) → L2 Redis → L3 database; over-invalidation wastes cache spend (more common), under-invalidation risks stale-data incidents; set TTL by data-class staleness tolerance
